To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the artificial legal distinctions that grew out of California water law's historical treatment of surface water and groundwater as separate resources can have legacy effects on groundwater management, and that the Sustainable Groundwater Management act's efforts to integrate science and law have only begun to address those legacy effects.

California's Sustainable Groundwater Management act (SGMA) is a partial integration of science and policy that has not yet fully addressed the legacy of an artificial legal divide between surface water and groundwater.

California's 2014 Sustainable Management Act (SGMCA) is a complex, multi-layered reform effort that is still in the process of addressing legacy effects of an artificial legal divide between surface and groundwater.
